title: Uncertainty Estimation via Hyperspherical Confidence Mapping
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A single deterministic uncertainty estimate separates noise-driven uncertainty inside the data region from model uncertainty outside it, and closely tracks the true noise level.
layout: 2 panels side by side with shared legend boxes on top, (a)/(b) labels below, each a 1-D line plot over x
description: Two side-by-side line plots, each with a legend box on top. Panel (a) is a 1-D regression toy. Black training points cluster near x in [-2,2]. A dashed red true cubic-like curve and a solid blue prediction run together near the data. Light-blue shaded uncertainty bands are narrow around the data, then fan out widely beyond the dashed gray vertical lines at x = ±4, so epistemic uncertainty grows outside the training domain. Panel (b) plots the ground-truth noise level sigma(x) as a solid blue line. It rises linearly from 0 at x = -2 to 20 at x = 2, then drops to zero. The estimated sigma-hat(x) is a dashed red curve that follows this ramp, with some underestimation near the peak and small bumps outside. The eye goes first to the widening blue fan in (a) and then to the two overlaid curves in (b).
caption: (a) Aleatoric uncertainty is captured in the noisy region ($x \in [-2,2]$), while epistemic uncertainty appears outside the training domain ($x \notin [-4,4]$). (b) $\hat\sigma(x)$ closely tracks the ground-truth $\sigma(x)$.
abstract: Quantifying uncertainty in neural network predictions is essential for high-stakes domains such as autonomous driving, healthcare, and manufacturing. While existing approaches often depend on costly sampling or restrictive distributional assumptions, we propose Hyperspherical Confidence Mapping (HCM), a simple yet principled framework for sampling-free and distribution-free uncertainty estimation. HCM decomposes outputs into a magnitude and a normalized direction vector constrained to lie on the unit hypersphere, enabling a novel interpretation of uncertainty as the degree of violation of this geometric constraint. This yields deterministic and interpretable estimates applicable to both regression and classification. Experiments across diverse benchmarks and real-world industrial tasks demonstrate that HCM matches or surpasses ensemble and evidential approaches, with far lower inference cost and stronger confidence-error alignment. Our results highlight the power of geometric structure in uncertainty estimation and position HCM as a versatile alternative to conventional techniques.
